paras: The lynching of John Harris took place on August 10, 1895, in western Colquitt County, Georgia, when a group of men killed Harris, an 18-year-old Black youth accused of assaulting an elderly white woman. Harris was captured near Camilla after a manhunt and shot to death on the way back to Colquitt County, though some reports said he had been burned or hanged. The story ran in papers across the country, often under headlines that approved the killing, and a Moultrie correspondent called it the county's first lynching.

On Friday, August 9, Harris was accused of attacking Mrs. John Monroe, a white woman reported as 60, 65 or 66 years old, at her home near Hurbfield Mill in Colquitt County. A dispatch from Camilla, sent as a special to the Atlanta Journal, called the crime an attempted assault and named the accused Will Harris. A special from Albany went further, saying that Harris choked the woman into insensibility and raped her, that neighbors who heard her screams saw him leave, and that she named him before dying a few hours later. The Moultrie correspondent of the Savannah Morning News described only an assault on an elderly white woman who later identified Harris.

Harris fled into Mitchell County, and according to the Albany special a posse of 200 men was soon in pursuit. He was captured near Camilla on Saturday, August 10. The Moultrie account, the most detailed and the only one written from Moultrie, said a bailiff from Colquitt County made the arrest and was taking Harris to the jail at Moultrie.

On Saturday morning, as they passed near the scene of the alleged crime about eleven miles from Moultrie, a number of unknown men took the prisoner from the bailiff and led him down the road. About half an hour later the bailiff heard several shots and, following the road, found Harris's body "riddled with shot." The Camilla dispatch likewise said Harris was taken to the scene "for confession" and shot to death by a mob, and several papers added that he confessed.

The bailiff went to Moultrie, reported the killing and asked for an inquest, and the coroner's jury returned a verdict that, according to the correspondent, matched his account. The coverage names no members of the party that killed Harris and reports no arrests. The correspondent wrote that the county's fair name had been "soiled" by its first lynching, but that the killing was taken as "a natural and inevitable consequence of the crime committed."

Two wire versions reached the white press on August 12 and 13. The short Camilla dispatch ran in papers from Raleigh and Wilmington to Salem, Oregon, where the Capital Journal headed it "Served Him Right." Others printed it under plain heads such as "Shot to Death by a Mob" and "Negro Lynched in Georgia," and weekly news summaries repeated it into late August.

The longer Albany special, relayed through Savannah, carried the rape and death accusations and the rumors of torture. The Savannah Morning News titled it "A Rapist's Fate" and said Harris's end "Might Well Deter Others," while the Sacramento Record-Union called it "A Brute Put to Death." The Birmingham Age-Herald asked "Burned or Cut into Bits?" and the San Francisco Call said he was "Said to Have Been Tortured to Death." The text itself called the reports of method conflicting, yet the Dawson News, a Georgia weekly, ran it on August 21 under the head "Burned at the Stake."
Throughout, the white papers called Harris a "brute" and a "fiend" and treated the accusation as proven. No coverage of the lynching was found in the Black press.

The reports disagree on Harris's first name, called Will or William in the Camilla dispatch and John in the Albany and Moultrie reports. They also disagree on how he died: the Camilla dispatch and the Moultrie letter say he was shot, while the Albany special passed on stories that he was burned, or cut, shot and hanged, without vouching for them.
Only the Albany special reported that Mrs. Monroe died, and one South Carolina brief dated the lynching to Sunday rather than Saturday.

reader.title: Lynching of John Harris
bases: A man accused of assaulting a white woman was seized after capture and killed by a mob or posse, by every account (A1, A7, A16).

All accounts agree Harris was killed by a 'mob' (A1) or by 'a number of unknown men' who took him from a bailiff (A16), after a 200-man posse hunt (A7), without trial, as punishment for an alleged assault on a white woman, which the Moultrie correspondent called 'a natural and inevitable consequence' (A16).

Three independent reports, the Atlanta Journal's Camilla special (A1, A9), the Albany special (A7, A3) and a Moultrie correspondent's letter (A16), agree that Harris was captured near Camilla on Saturday and killed by a group of men, though they differ on his first name, the method of killing and the custody.

accounts.label: Camilla dispatch (Atlanta Journal special)
accounts.gist: Will Harris, who 'attempted' to assault Mrs. J. F. Monroe, 60, on Friday, was captured at Camilla on Saturday, taken to the scene of the crime for confession, and shot to death by a mob.

accounts.label: Albany special via Savannah
accounts.gist: John Harris, 18, choked and raped Mrs. John Monroe, who died hours later after naming him; a 200-man posse captured him near Camilla, and on the way back to Colquitt County he was 'disposed of', by reports either burned or cut, shot and hanged.

accounts.label: Moultrie correspondent
accounts.gist: A Colquitt bailiff captured Harris in Mitchell County; on Saturday morning, near the scene of the crime, unknown men took him from the bailiff, and half an hour later his body was found riddled with shot; a coroner's jury investigated.

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News ran the Albany special as 'A Rapist's Fate', an end that 'Might Well Deter Others', and its Moultrie correspondent called the lynching a 'natural and inevitable consequence'.
The Salem Capital Journal headed the Camilla wire 'Served Him Right.'

Papers carrying the Albany special used 'Brute', 'Fiendish Negro' and 'Brutal Negro' in headlines and text, and the Dawson News headlined it 'Burned at the Stake' though its text called the method unconfirmed.
Raleigh, Wilmington and Roanoke papers printed the Camilla dispatch under neutral heads such as 'Shot to Death by a Mob' and 'Negro Lynched in Georgia'.

conflicts.note: Both versions describe one man accused of the same act against Mrs. Monroe; the local Moultrie letter and the Albany special agree on John.
